Zdrada stanu w polskim prawie to najcięższe przestępstwo polityczne, polegające na działaniu na szkodę Rzeczypospolitej Polskiej, w tym dążeniu do pozbawienia jej niepodległości, uszczuplenia terytorium lub zamachu na jej bezpieczeństwo. Jest spenalizowana w Kodeksie karnym jako szereg zbrodni, a nie jeden, konkretny czyn.

Do najpoważniejszych czynów kwalifikowanych jako zdrada stanu należą:
• Zdrada dyplomatyczna (art. 129 KK): Działanie na szkodę RP przez osobę upoważnioną do występowania w imieniu państwa w stosunkach z rządem obcego państwa lub organizacją zagraniczną.
• Szpiegostwo (art. 130 KK): Udział w działalności obcego wywiadu przeciwko RP.
• Zamach stanu (art. 127 KK): Usiłowanie zmiany przemocą konstytucyjnych organów RP.
• Działania przeciwko niepodległości lub terytorium: Udział w działalności zmierzającej do pozbawienia RP suwerenności lub oderwania części jej terytorium.

Zdrada stanu jest zbrodnią zagrożoną surowymi karami pozbawienia wolności, w tym karą do 25 lat lub dożywocia w przypadku najcięższych zamachów na bezpieczeństwo państwa.

Dr. Brad is very sympathetic character, but not a stellar scientist. What is the problem? He extrapolates UNSCIENTIFICALLY beyond what the study actually shows. The study shows that rapamycin 6mg once a week will tend to blunt muscle growth/performance when exercised over 13 weeks. That's it. Sum total. Nothing more. To say that this tells us ANYTHING about rapamycin as a longevity drug is extrapolation which is not justified by the study. First, exercise performance is not a good metric of longevity. In fact, it is a very poor metric. Exercise does not extend max lifespan, it only lowers mortality, we've seen this in many animal experiments. A mouse that lives 950 days on average has a greater chance of living 950 days when exercised (insted of dying at, say 600 days), but it will not make it live to 1200 days like rapamycin does. So, exercise is not a longevity extender. Second, there is a trade off as you intimated between exercise performance and longevity - we've seen this in many animal studies, especially CR (caloric restriction). The *longest* (exceeding max lifespan) lived animals were the most restricted and if given more calories so they had the energy to exercise, lived shorter lifespans. And all CR'd animals (even mildly CR'd) had worse exercise performance. Animals on CR have weaker muscles (and bones), but live longer. Btw., look at supercentenarians (and centenarians) - you will not find enthusiastic exercisers overrepresented among them. If exercise was the ticket, you'd have all centenarians or more of them be gym rats, instead, their exercise habits are no different than the rest of the population. What does both CR and rapamycin do? Extend max lifespan in all species studied. What do CR'd animals (and now apparently rapamycin exposed too) have in common? Lower exercise performance - not surprising since both suppress mTOR. So to say, as Brad does, that exercise performance is a good marker of longevity - is simply WRONG. Furthermore, it's NOT SCIENTIFICALLY SUPPORTED to say that maybe more spread out rapamycin dosing will work better - because we may WANT to have greater exposure, since the premise itself (that blunting exercise through mTOR suppression is a longevity negative) is faulty.

This of course doesn't mean rapamycin will be a net positive for longevity in humans - there is no way to prove it. CR works in all animals studied, but longevity in humans will never be an RCT trial, at best we have biomarkers (and not just one performance metric like exercise) - still imperfect, but there was a human trial of CR, called CALERIE (look it up), where humans did dramatically better on CR (except for bone and muscle!). Same for rapamycin - it works to extend max lifespan in all species studied so far (including monkeys - marmosets), so the gamble is "why would it suddenly stop working in humans?". That's a gamble, not science, but a gamble that some of us think have pretty good odds worth taking a chance on depending on your risk tolerance. We gamble that a drug that works in all species studied will not suddenly stop working in humans - of course, we may be tragically wrong.

One other note on exercise performance. Animals on CR have interesting results on many markers - initially they are worse, but they are beneficial in the long run. Example, testosterone levels on CR drop dramatically... but then stabilize and by old age maintain HIGHER testosterone levels than controls. The same is speculated about muscle and bone. Muscle may be less in volume and strength initially, but will have better quality of performance in old age; bone density may be lesser on CR, but it's speculated that the architecture of the bone is superior, so paradoxically it will last longer in old age. Of course some of this is not slam dunk proven (like with bone health), but it's a possibility. Finally, yes, there may be downsides to rapamycin - perhaps glucose or lipid control etc., but that's where you either take the trade off, OR as many of us do, you counter it by other drugs, just as a lifesaving cancer drug has side effects which can be ameliorated with other drugs. Same here. Perhaps, you may need to exercise a bit more on rapamycin to get the same benefits than those who are not on rapamycin, but so what? It's just a way to ameliorate the downsides while keeping the upsides.

The Facts on China's Hantavirus Vaccine
When it was made: The first hantavirus vaccine used in China was developed and licensed in 1990.  

What it is: It is an inactivated vaccine (killed virus) derived from either rodent brains or cell cultures. It was specifically designed to target the Hantaan River virus and the Seoul virus, which cause Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS).  

Usage: It is widely used within China, with an estimated two million doses administered annually. Research suggests its use contributed to a massive drop in hantavirus cases in the country—from over 100,000 cases per year in the 1980s to less than 20,000 by 2007.  

Why is it not used globally?
If you're in the US, Europe, or Australia, you won't find this vaccine at your local clinic. There are a few reasons for this:

Regional Strains: The Chinese vaccine targets the "Old World" hantaviruses (HFRS). In the Americas, the "New World" strains (like Sin Nombre virus) cause Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS), which is a different disease. The Chinese vaccine doesn't protect against these American strains.

Regulatory Approval: The vaccine has never undergone the rigorous clinical trial process required by the FDA (USA) or EMA (Europe).

Efficiency Concerns: International health organizations like the WHO have noted that while the vaccine is used locally, there are still questions regarding exactly how long its protection lasts and how effective it is across all variants.  

Current Status (2026)
As of early May 2026, there has been renewed interest in hantavirus vaccines due to small outbreaks in Europe and South America. While scientists at the University of Bath and other institutions are currently working on a modern, "universal" hantavirus vaccine, the original inactivated versions remain largely confined to China and South Korea.

Hidup dan mati sudah bagian perjalanan manusia di bumi.apapun yg pernah hidup psti bakal mati.

Meskipun "AstraZeneca" terdengar seperti satu kata Latin yang kuno, nama ini sebenarnya adalah gabungan dari dua kata (hasil merger perusahaan Swedia dan Inggris) yang memiliki akar bahasa berbeda.

Berikut adalah bedah maknanya:

1. Astra
Kata ini berasal dari bahasa Latin "Astrum", yang berarti:

Bintang

Benda langit

Kejayaan atau ketinggian (dalam konteks puitis)

2. Zeneca
Bagian ini sebenarnya bukan bahasa Latin asli. "Zeneca" adalah nama buatan yang dirancang oleh agensi branding untuk perusahaan Inggris (ICI Pharmaceuticals) sebelum bergabung dengan Astra.

Secara linguistik, "Zene-" mungkin diambil dari bahasa Yunani "Xenos" yang berarti asing atau baru.

Namun, tujuan utamanya adalah agar nama tersebut mudah diucapkan di berbagai bahasa dan terdengar futuristik.
